name: Codeine
summary: Codeine does almost nothing by itself. It works only to the extent that your liver converts it to morphine, and the enzyme that does this varies more between people than almost any other in pharmacology. Depending on genes you may have inherited, the same tablet is a placebo, a painkiller, or a dangerous dose of morphine.
mechanism: A prodrug. About 5-10% is O-demethylated by CYP2D6 into morphine, which does all the analgesic work. The rest is converted into inactive products. CYP2D6 activity is genetically determined and spans a huge range: roughly 5-10% of people of European descent are poor metabolizers and get essentially no pain relief, while ultrarapid metabolizers — up to 1-2% in Europe but as high as 15-30% in parts of North Africa and the Arabian peninsula — can produce several times the expected morphine.

oral.note: The usual route. Well absorbed, but what matters is not how much codeine arrives — it is how much of it the liver turns into morphine.

pathways.name: Codeine-6-glucuronide
pathways.note: The bulk of it, and inactive. Most of a codeine dose simply never becomes a painkiller.

pathways.name: Morphine (via CYP2D6)
pathways.note: The entire effect, from under a tenth of the dose. This fraction is what varies between people: near zero in poor metabolizers, several times higher in ultrarapid metabolizers.

cyp2d6_poor.note: Poor metabolizers — around 5-10% of people of European descent — convert almost no codeine to morphine and get little or no pain relief, while still getting the nausea and constipation. Increasing the dose does not help; it just adds side effects.

cyp2d6_ultrarapid.note: Ultrarapid metabolizers produce far more morphine than expected from the same dose. This caused deaths in children given codeine after tonsillectomy, and in at least one breastfed infant whose mother was an ultrarapid metabolizer — which is why codeine is now contraindicated in children and in breastfeeding.

risk: You cannot tell which metabolizer type you are without a test. If codeine has never worked for you, that is likely genetic, and taking more will not change it.
Ultrarapid metabolizers face the opposite problem: an ordinary dose can produce morphine levels associated with respiratory depression.
CYP2D6 inhibitors — fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine — convert a normal metabolizer into a functional poor metabolizer, so codeine stops working while someone is on them.
Combination tablets with paracetamol set a hard ceiling: taking more for pain relief risks paracetamol liver injury long before it improves the opioid effect. See interactions.
